claims.text: The studied system is a FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy-alloy coating on a Cu matrix.
The FeNiCrCoCu coating has an FCC structure.
At 300 K, the coating has high dislocation density and stable stacking-fault structures.
At 300 K, the coating exhibits stable wear resistance and high elastic modulus.
Frictional heating can significantly raise the contact temperature.
A thermally activated reduction in stacking-fault energy drives the transition from stable to unstable wear.
A reduction in stacking-fault energy suppresses deformation twinning and promotes dislocation climb and cross-slip.
At room temperature, high lattice distortion and low stacking-fault energy promote deformation twinning and stable stacking-fault networks.
Twin boundaries and stacking-fault networks impede dislocation motion and thereby maintain hardness and wear resistance.
Stacking-fault energy rises as temperature increases.
Rising stacking-fault energy suppresses twinning and lowers the critical stress for dislocation cross-slip and climb.
Enhanced dislocation mobility causes dislocation annihilation and cell formation, producing lattice softening.
Elevated contact temperature softens the alloy and increases its wear rate.
Thermal energy overcomes defect-migration barriers associated with lattice distortion and accelerates atomic disorder.
Breakdown of the protective oxide film contributes to the sharp decline in wear resistance.
A critical temperature exists at which the wear rate increases by an order of magnitude.
Below the critical temperature, wear is dominated by mild abrasive and adhesive mechanisms with a stable subsurface microstructure.
Above the critical temperature, wear shifts to severe oxidative and adhesive modes.
Above the critical temperature, dislocation density rapidly saturates.
Above the critical temperature, twin boundaries are lost and rapid lattice disorder develops.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis attributes the transition to a thermally activated reduction in stacking-fault energy, whereas the mechanism states that stacking-fault energy rises with temperature.
